title: Composition and slicing

youtube.title: C++ Composition vs Inheritance and Object Slicing | C++ Programming EP 68
youtube.description: In this episode you will choose between has-a and is-a, build a class from parts and avoid object slicing, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Composition and slicing · 0:52 A car has an engine · 1:32 Is-a or has-a? · 2:02 Second program · 3:02 Recap · 3:32 Bug of the Day · 4:20 Challenge · 4:40 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "HAS-A OR IS-A" in tomato on pastel blue; Xecxec next to a car with an engine inside it; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a car with an engine inside it

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we choose the right tool for the design. We also meet slicing, a bug that cuts your object in half.

scenes.onScreen: "Composition and slicing": numbered lines (1. Is-a means inheritance; 2. Has-a means composition; 3. Pass polymorphic objects by reference, never by value) and an analogy card: a car and its engine: a car has an engine, it is not an engine
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Use inheritance for an is-a relationship. A dog is an animal. Use composition for a has-a relationship. A car has an engine. Composition makes a member out of another class. Prefer composition when you are not sure. It is simpler. A second danger is slicing. Passing a derived object by value to a base parameter cuts off the derived part. Pass by reference.
points: Pass polymorphic objects by reference, never by value

analogy.title: Composition and slicing
analogy.body: A car and its engine: a car has an engine, it is not an engine

scenes.onScreen: car.cpp: Car contains an Engine as a member
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Engine is a small class with one job. [HL 10] Car has an engine as a member. This is composition. [HL 13] Drive uses the engine. [HL 14] It calls start on the member. [HL 20] Main makes a car. [HL 21] The output shows the engine start, and then the car moves.

scenes.onScreen: a table of examples and the right tool
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Use the sentence test. If the sentence says is a, use inheritance. If it says has a, use composition. A dog is an animal. A car has an engine. When in doubt, choose composition.

diagram.caption: a table of examples and the right tool

scenes.onScreen: slice.cpp: a derived object is passed by value and loses its derived part
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 14] This function takes an Animal by value. The compiler copies only the Animal part of the dog. The Dog part is sliced off. [HL 15] This one takes a reference. No copy is made. [HL 19] The first call prints three dots. [HL 20] The second call prints Woof. Always pass polymorphic objects by reference or by pointer.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as slice dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints three dots, and then Woof.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Use inheritance for is-a. Two. Use composition for has-a. Three. When in doubt, prefer composition. Four. Pass polymorphic objects by reference, never by value. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Pass polymorphic objects by reference, never by value.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Slicing in a function call
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We pass a Dog to a function that takes an Animal by value. The function prints three dots, not Woof. The Dog part was sliced off in the copy. Take a const reference instead.

scenes.onScreen: Object slicing is a bad deal. You asked for a whole dog, and you got half a dog.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Object slicing is a bad deal. You asked for a whole dog, and you got half a dog.

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class Computer that has a Processor and a Memory as members. Add a function that starts both. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: We end module seven here. Next time: templates, code that works for any type. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.why: Passing by value copies only the Animal part of the Dog. The copy is a plain Animal, so speak prints three dots.

pun: "Object slicing is a bad deal. You asked for a whole dog, and you got half a dog."
challenge: Write a class Computer that has a Processor and a Memory as members. Add a function that starts both.
challengeAnswer: Make Processor and Memory small classes with a start function. In Computer, keep one of each as a member. The start function calls both.
